summary: Describes Cooperating Layered Architecture for Software-Defined Networking (CLAS), an architecture that splits control functions into cooperating layers instead of one tightly integrated vertical entity. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Rather than one boss controlling a network, there are layers of managers, each doing its own part and talking to each other.

questions: cooperating layered architecture for software-defined networking
separating service and transport in sdn
subtitle: Split network control into separate layers for services and transport.

tldr.problem: Software-Defined Networking (SDN) typically centralizes all control functions in a single monolithic controller. This tightly couples transport control (routing, forwarding) with service control (VoIP, video, etc.), making it hard to manage them independently, scale, troubleshoot, or set business boundaries between providers.
tldr.mechanism: CLAS proposes splitting the centralized control into two separate, cooperating layers: a Service Stratum for service-related functions and a Transport Stratum for connectivity. Each has its own control, management, and resource planes. The Service Stratum acts as a client of the Transport Stratum, requesting transport capabilities through standard interfaces.
tldr.outcome: Services and transport can evolve independently, be maintained by different teams, scale separately, and be clearly allocated between providers. The standard interfaces between layers enable interoperability and reduce coupling.

today: RFC 8597 is an Informational RFC published in May 2019 and is not obsoleted. It describes the CLAS concept as a reference architecture for SDN designs. Related frameworks like ACTN (RFC 8453) implement similar layered approaches in specific contexts.

sections.title: The Case for Layered Control
sections.content:
Software-Defined Networking separates the control plane from the data plane, moving control logic to a central SDN Controller. This is powerful, but typical SDN designs treat the controller as a monolith containing all control functions: forwarding, routing, service provisioning, VoIP setup, video delivery, and more. This vertical, tightly integrated approach creates problems. Different departments in a provider (transport teams, service teams) have unclear responsibilities. Troubleshooting is hard because it is unclear which layer caused a failure. Complex services cannot reuse transport functions. And business boundaries blur when different providers are involved.

CLAS addresses this by separating transport control from service control into distinct, cooperating layers, inspired by the ITU-T Next Generation Network (Y.2011) architecture.
sections.eli5: Normal SDN puts everything in one control box. CLAS says split the box in two: one part controls the network plumbing, the other controls the services running on top. They cooperate but stay separate.

sections.title: The CLAS Layered Architecture
sections.content:
CLAS defines two functional strata, each with SDN Intelligence (control, management, and resource planes):

Transport Stratum: Contains functions focused on transferring data between endpoints. The control plane instructs forwarding devices to build data paths. The management plane handles fault and performance management. The resource plane is the physical forwarding nodes and network infrastructure.

Service Stratum: Contains functions for providing services and capabilities to applications. The control plane configures service resources (computing, databases) and requests transport capabilities from the Transport Stratum. The management plane operates the service resources and coordinates with Transport management. The resource plane includes servers, storage, registries, and other service-related assets.

The two strata communicate through standard, open interfaces. The Service Stratum acts as a client requesting transport capabilities; the Transport Stratum provides those capabilities and can notify the Service Stratum of underlying transport events.
sections.eli5: Imagine a network as two shops sharing a building: one runs the heating and electricity (Transport), the other runs the retail store (Service). Each has its own manager and staff. The retail manager asks the facilities manager 'I need power for three rooms.' The facilities manager says 'OK, I've got that.' If something breaks, you know which manager to call.

sections.title: Planes and Responsibilities
sections.content:
Each stratum divides its functions into three planes:

Control Plane: Logically centralizes and directs control functions. In the Transport Stratum, it instructs forwarding devices on how to handle traffic. In the Service Stratum, it configures service resources and requests transport.

Management Plane: Centralizes management (FCAPS: Fault, Configuration, Accounting, Performance, Security). Monitors devices, tracks resource use, and ensures policy compliance.

Resource Plane: The actual resources being controlled. For transport, these are forwarding nodes and links. For services, these are servers, databases, and application components.

The planes within each stratum can interact with corresponding planes in the other stratum, enabling inter-layer cooperation. For example, the Service Control Plane can request transport resources from the Transport Control Plane, and the Transport Management Plane can alert the Service Management Plane about link failures.
sections.eli5: Each stratum is like a small company with three departments: Strategy (control), Compliance (management), and Warehouse (resources). The Strategy departments of both companies talk to each other to make deals.

sections.title: Required Features and Communication
sections.content:
For CLAS to work, several features are essential: Abstraction maps physical resources into abstract views. Service-Parameter Translation converts service requirements (SLA terms like latency) into transport capabilities. Monitoring provides real-time updates on resource status. Resource Computation decides which resources to use for requests. Orchestration combines diverse resources efficiently. Accounting tracks resource usage, and Security protects communication between controllers.

The Service Stratum SDN Intelligence must easily access transport resources through well-defined APIs. The Transport Stratum must capture Service requirements precisely. Communication must be secure, preventing denial-of-service attacks. The two strata must also agree on how to map service-level SLAs (e.g., 'end-to-end delay under 50ms') to transport-level SLAs.
sections.eli5: The two managers need to understand each other's language. 'I need fast delivery' (service) must translate to 'low-latency paths' (transport). They also need secure phones so nobody can trick one into making bad decisions.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
CLAS applies to multiple scenarios. Full SDN environments have both strata SDN-enabled. One Transport Stratum can serve multiple Service Strata (one company's infrastructure supporting many service providers). Or one Service Stratum can use multiple Transport Strata (one service provider buying connectivity from multiple carriers).

Hybrid environments mix SDN and legacy systems. An SDN Service Stratum can work with a legacy Transport Stratum through an adapter. Or an SDN Transport Stratum can serve a legacy Service Stratum. Multi-domain scenarios occur when the Transport Stratum spans multiple administrative domains (different companies or geographic regions). In these cases, one Transport controller can abstract multiple underlying domains, presenting a single interface to the Service Stratum.
sections.eli5: The setup can be flexible: both companies SDN-enabled, or one SDN and one old-fashioned, or the transport side managing multiple companies' networks.

sections.title: Challenges and Scope
sections.content:
Implementing CLAS raises several challenges. There is no single standard protocol yet for Service-to-Transport communication; candidates include I-CPI (Intermediate-Controller Plane Interface), TAPI (Transport API), and CPNP (Connectivity Provisioning Negotiation Protocol). Multi-domain awareness complicates matters: the Service Stratum may or may not know about multiple transport providers, changing who is responsible for orchestrating end-to-end paths. SLA mapping between service and transport requires careful specification. Secure, authenticated communication with message integrity is essential. And accounting systems must track resource use across strata.

RFC 8597 documents the CLAS concept and challenges but does not mandate specific solutions. It also acknowledges related work, particularly RFC 7426 (SDN terminology and architecture) and RFC 8453 (Abstraction and Control of TE Networks, ACTN), which implements similar layering concepts.
sections.eli5: It's tricky to make two independent managers work together. Who talks to whom? What language do they use? How do we trust each other? The RFC describes the problems without dictating a single answer.
